analysis.one_liner: Gives the president authority to negotiate trade deals that Congress can approve or reject, but not amend.
analysis.headline: The Senate Finance Committee reported the bill in May 2015 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but no floor vote is recorded and the Congress ended with it never enacted.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would renew what is known as "trade promotion authority" or "fast track." It lets the president negotiate big trade agreements — like the Trans-Pacific Partnership — and then bring the finished deal to Congress for a simple yes-or-no vote, with no amendments allowed and limited debate, guaranteeing the deal gets a vote by a set deadline. In exchange, the bill spells out negotiating goals the administration must pursue, such as opening foreign markets to U.S. exports, protecting intellectual property, addressing currency manipulation, and respecting labor and environmental standards, and it adds consultation and transparency requirements. Deals under negotiation with Pacific Rim countries and the European Union would be covered.
analysis.who_benefits: Export-oriented businesses — manufacturers, farmers, technology firms, and pharmaceutical, entertainment, and other intellectual-property-heavy companies — would gain the most, because the president would get streamlined power to finish trade agreements that lower foreign tariffs and strengthen patent and copyright rules abroad. The administration would also gain, since trade agreements negotiated under this bill would come to Congress under special fast-track procedures that prevent amendments and force a vote. Congress as an institution would receive new consultation rights and access to negotiating documents, and the public would get formal transparency mechanisms at the trade office.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes the president to negotiate and sign agreements lowering tariffs and other trade barriers through mid-2018 (extendable to 2021), with special expedited procedures that let implementing bills come to the floor in each chamber without amendment and with limited debate.

Sets detailed negotiating objectives favoring expanded market access for U.S. goods, services, agriculture, and intellectual-property holders, including strong enforcement of patents and copyrights abroad and disciplines on foreign government price controls that affect U.S. products such as pharmaceuticals.

Adds oversight features relative to prior fast-track law: congressional advisory groups with access to negotiating documents, designated congressional advisers, public consultation guidelines, and a new Chief Transparency Officer at the USTR to consult with Congress and engage the public.

analysis.who_pays: Workers in import-competing industries — manufacturing, apparel, textiles — would bear the risk of trade agreements negotiated under the bill, since the same deals that open foreign markets also lower barriers to imports and are historically associated with job displacement. The bill would also bind Congress: on any finished trade deal, members could not offer amendments, only an up-or-down vote. Consumers and future users of medicines could pay more under provisions pushing stronger intellectual-property protections and opposing foreign drug price controls.
analysis.who_pays_short: Import-competing workers and members of Congress

drawbacks.text: The bill would let the president sign trade agreements before Congress votes on them, and then force Congress to consider implementing bills under special fast-track procedures — a limited-amendment process that allows only a yes-or-no vote, with no opportunity to fix individual provisions of a finished agreement.

The bill directs negotiators to seek investor-state dispute mechanisms and strong intellectual-property protections, provisions that critics have long argued let companies challenge domestic health and safety rules and extend patent and copyright protections at consumers' expense. Labor and environment objectives are framed as negotiating goals, not guarantees, with parties allowed broad 'bona fide' discretion in enforcing their own labor laws.

The negotiating objectives aim to bar foreign price controls and reference pricing for pharmaceuticals, a provision that could make medicines more expensive abroad and reduce the pressure on drug prices in the United States.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If it had passed, the benefits would have flowed mainly to export industries, multinational firms, and intellectual-property holders, in the form of a streamlined path for trade deals that Congress could not amend. The costs would have fallen on anyone whose job, wage, or access to affordable medicine is affected by the terms of those deals — and the bill's own structure (no amendments, one up-or-down vote) made it harder for Congress to fix harmful terms later. The transparency additions in the reported version were real but modest compared with the negotiating authority being granted.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Finance Committee approved the bill with amendments and put it on the Senate calendar, but no vote was ever taken on it and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 16, 2015 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
On April 22, 2015 the Finance Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with amendments, and on May 11, 2015 Chairman Hatch reported it to the Senate with amendments.

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on May 11, 2015, where it awaited a floor vote that never occurred; the Congress ended on January 3, 2017 with the bill never enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the streamlined fast-track route for trade deals it would have created was not established through this bill. Industries counting on it to finalize trade agreements lost that path; critics of fast-track, including labor groups, came out ahead in the narrow sense that the negotiating authority was not renewed through this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of the trade negotiating authority

for.name: Orrin Hatch
for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah and Chairman of the Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, reported it out of the Finance Committee with amendments, and placed it on the Senate calendar.

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole Democratic cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: Senate Committee on Finance
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported favorably with amendments on April 22, 2015 and reported it on May 11, 2015.

against.name: Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Widely reported at the time: blocked the bill's floor consideration in May 2015 to leverage a companion worker-assistance bill, stalling the trade agenda.

against.name: Organized labor and allied advocacy groups
against.what_they_did: Ran public campaigns against fast-track authority, arguing it would lock in trade deals that cost manufacturing jobs.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a bipartisan effort — a Republican chairman with the committee's senior Democrat as its cosponsor — while opposition came largely from other Democrats, a split visible in the record only through the committee's filed Minority views and, outside the record, in the Senate floor standoff of May 2015.

industries.note: Fast-track authority makes trade agreements like the Trans-Pacific Partnership achievable, locking in tariff reductions and market access abroad. Without it, other countries do not put their final offers on the table.

The bill instructs negotiators to seek patent and copyright protections matching U.S. law and to fight foreign drug price controls. Stronger IP terms abroad raise returns for patent- and copyright-heavy firms, at some cost to medicine access.
Objectives target reducing foreign tariffs and subsidies on farm goods, though with protections for import-sensitive U.S. farm products. Gains would flow mainly to larger commodity producers.

Organized labor opposed fast-track legislation because deals negotiated under it historically lacked enforceable labor standards and accelerated offshoring. The bill's labor provisions are negotiating goals, not binding guarantees.

Objectives support free cross-border data flows and a moratorium on internet tariffs, which benefits tech firms; the same provisions would restrict governments' ability to regulate data localization and privacy locally.
